news.title: School phone bans work, but don’t expect straight-A students overnight
news.summary: Taking smartphones away from students during the school day might actually help them learn a little more. A new Harvard-led study covering 3.3 million students across 4,600 US schools found that strict cellphone restrictions resulted in modest improvements in academic performance. The gains are equivalent to roughly one or two additional weeks of learning over a school year, suggesting that keeping phones out of classrooms can help, even if it isn't going to transform grades overnight. Published by Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research in partnership with researchers from NWEA and Dartmouth, the study examined math and reading progress among students in grades 3 through 10. It analysed data collected between the 2021-22 and 2025-26 school years, comparing academic growth before and after schools introduced strict phone restrictions. news.title: America’s AI agents may be helping their biggest competitors without realizing it
news.summary: The race to build the world's most powerful AI models is getting increasingly competitive, and China has found an interesting way to keep up with its American rivals. Rather than relying entirely on expensive chips and building everything from scratch, Chinese developers are using answers generated by leading US AI models to improve their own systems. According to a new Reuters investigation, which examined more than 300 academic papers, patents, company records, and government documents, this approach has become increasingly common across China's AI industry. It's another development in a market where Chinese AI companies already compete aggressively on pricing. The technique is called AI distillation, and while it isn't new or inherently illegal, the scale at which Chinese companies are reportedly adopting it is raising concerns in Washington. Think of distillation as a student learning from a more experienced teacher.

news.title: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?
news.summary: Photograph: Darrell Jackson Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree. As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai. Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

news.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI.

news.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it

One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe.

news.title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
news.summary: With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI. It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates.

news.title: No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?
news.summary: Animation: Timo Lenzen On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.” New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway.

If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week, Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.” In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover.
